added_claims.speaker: Scott Bessent
added_claims.quote: there's complete mobility of Labor there was a Cal government that could smooth over and like you know this doesn't didn't exist
added_claims.claim: The US absorbs regional shocks (1980s Texas energy bust) through labour mobility and federal fiscal transfers; the ERM/euro area had mobile capital but neither, which is why the currency arrangement was structurally flawed.
added_claims.direction: currency unions without fiscal union are fragile
added_claims.conditions: when member economies are structured very differently
added_claims.testable: partly - historical analogue, not a signal

added_claims.testable: partly - positioning and skew data allow tests

corrections.issue: Speaker is probably wrong: the remark about a unified currency with mobile capital and different economies comes in Bessent's own reply (continuing his 'systems that accelerate and break down' framing and his 1980s US anecdote), not from host Ash Bennington. The claim also omits the labour-mobility/fiscal-transfer contrast he draws.
corrections.fix: Bessent: a currency arrangement that joins very mobile capital with structurally different economies is a flawed system, unlike the US where labour mobility and federal transfers smooth shocks.

completeness_estimate: 0.90 - the first reader captured the ERM, asymmetry, French election, China, gold, US debt, Japan and bifurcated-economy arguments; missed the epistemic-humility rule, the 'acceleration not cause' point on 1992, the labour-mobility/fiscal-union contrast, the behavioural-edge framing, the decoupling timing view, the Abenomics example and the Japanese-repatriation funding risk; one speaker misattribution.
